parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a letting agency about renting a flat.
script: Good morning, Castle Lettings, Hannah speaking.
Hi. I'm looking for a flat to rent, and I saw your website.
Let me take some details. What's your name?
Kenji Matsuda. That's M, A, T, S, U, D, A.
Thank you. What size of flat are you looking for?
Two bedrooms. I live alone, but I work from home some days, so I need a second room as an office.
Somewhere near the hospital. I'm a researcher there, and I'd like to be able to walk to work.
Up to nine hundred pounds a month.
Is there anything that's essential for you?
I'd love a garden, but I know that's unrealistic in the city centre. A balcony at least, please.
And when do you want to move in?
My current contract ends in August, so from the first of September.

I have two flats that might suit you. The first is on Elm Street, about ten minutes' walk from the hospital. It has two bedrooms and a balcony, and it's eight hundred and fifty a month. The only drawback is that there's no dishwasher.
The second is in Riverside Court. It's slightly bigger and newer, and the rent is nine hundred and twenty.
That's a bit over my budget.
Yes, but internet is included in the rent, which would save you about thirty pounds a month.
Oh, so it works out about the same. Could I see both?
Of course. How about Saturday? I could show you Elm Street at ten and Riverside Court at eleven.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide introduces visitors to a science museum.
script: Good morning, and welcome to the Northbridge Science Museum. I'm Peter, and I'm going to give you a quick introduction before you start exploring.

As some of you may know, the museum has just reopened after an eighteen-month renovation. The building is the same size as before, but the biggest change is that most exhibits are now hands-on. In the past, visitors could only look at objects behind glass.
Entry to the permanent galleries is still free, as are the gardens. However, there is a charge for the shows in the planetarium.
Please note that today we're closing at five o'clock, not at seven as usual, because there's a private event this evening.
Large bags and backpacks must be left in the lockers, which you'll find next to the main entrance. Small handbags are fine.
Now, where to find things. Here on the ground floor, you'll find the children's play zone, which is designed for under-sevens, and the shop, which is just by the exit.
The planetarium is downstairs in the basement. Shows start every hour.
On the first floor, you'll find our special exhibition on robots, which runs until the end of the year.
And on the second floor there are two galleries: the human body gallery, where you can see how your heart and lungs work, and the weather lab, where you can create your own small tornado.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two geography students, Ruth and Ahmed, plan a report on a river field trip.
script: Ruth, shall we plan the report on our river field trip?
Sure. What did you think of the trip overall?
I enjoyed it, but I felt we didn't have enough time at each site. We really rushed the measurements.
I agree. At least the weather was fine. What surprised me was how much faster the water was at the second site, even though the river was wider there.
Yes, I'd expected it to slow down. Now, Dr Kumar said the report shouldn't just describe the trip. The main focus should be comparing the three sites.
OK. Should we include the data from the other group?
I don't think so. They measured the speed using a different method, so the results can't really be compared with ours.
Fair enough. Who's going to draw the maps?
I'm hopeless at drawing. Could you do them? I'll do all the graphs.
Deal. Let's check our notes. At site one, the river was four and a half metres wide, and we measured the depth with a pole.
And for speed, we timed how long an orange took to float ten metres.
At site two, the river was seven metres wide, and the water temperature was fourteen degrees.
Site three was the one with all the pebbles on the river bed.
Right. And that's where we found a high level of fertiliser in the water, probably from the farm next to it.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture about sleep and memory.
script: Good morning. Today we're looking at the relationship between sleep and memory. For a long time, scientists believed that sleep was simply a time for rest, when the brain more or less switched off. We now know that this is far from true.

During deep sleep, the brain is extremely active. It appears to replay the experiences of the day and transfer memories from the hippocampus, which acts as a short-term store, to the cortex, where long-term memories are kept.

Some of the clearest evidence comes from studies of rats. When rats learned to run through a maze, particular brain cells fired in a certain pattern. Remarkably, the same pattern appeared again while the rats were asleep, as if they were practising the route.

The other main type of sleep, REM sleep, when most dreaming happens, seems to be important for emotional memories and for creativity. People woken from REM sleep often perform better on puzzles that require unusual solutions.
You don't necessarily need a full night's sleep to benefit. In one German study, even a nap of just six minutes improved people's ability to recall a list of words.
The reverse is also true. Research suggests that one night without sleep can reduce the brain's ability to form new memories by around forty percent.

This is particularly relevant for teenagers, whose body clocks shift later during adolescence, so they naturally fall asleep and wake up later. Some schools that have moved their start time later have reported better grades and fewer students falling asleep in class.
So what practical advice can we give? Avoid caffeine in the afternoon, stop using screens an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool and dark.

passages.title: The Journey of Tea
paragraphs: According to a popular Chinese legend, tea was discovered in 2737 BC by the emperor Shennong, when leaves from a nearby bush blew into a pot of water he was boiling. There is no historical evidence for the story, but there is no doubt that tea, made from the leaves of the plant Camellia sinensis, has been drunk in China for thousands of years, first as a medicine and later as an everyday drink.

By the time of the Tang dynasty, tea had become central to Chinese culture. In the eighth century the writer Lu Yu produced The Classic of Tea, the first book devoted entirely to the subject, which described how tea should be grown, prepared and served. Around the same period, Buddhist monks carried tea from China to Japan, where it later developed into the elaborate tea ceremony.

Tea did not reach Europe until the early seventeenth century, when it was brought by Dutch traders. In Britain it was at first an expensive luxury, but it became fashionable at the royal court after the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza, a keen tea drinker, married King Charles II in 1662. Over the following century, tea spread from the wealthy to ordinary households, and Britain became one of the world's largest consumers.

For a long time, all of this tea came from China, and the British East India Company held a monopoly on the trade. Concerned about depending on a single supplier, the company decided to grow tea in its Indian territories. In 1848 it sent the Scottish plant collector Robert Fortune into China, where he travelled in disguise and smuggled out thousands of tea plants and seeds. He also persuaded skilled tea workers to travel to India to teach their methods.

At the same time, the British had discovered a native tea plant growing wild in Assam, in north-east India. This turned out to be a different variety from the Chinese plant, with larger leaves and a stronger flavour, and it was well suited to the hot, wet climate. Plantations spread rapidly across Assam and into the nearby Sylhet region, where the first commercial tea garden opened in 1854. In Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, planters switched to tea after a disease destroyed the island's coffee crops in the 1870s.

The success of these plantations came at a heavy human cost. Hundreds of thousands of workers were brought from other regions under harsh contracts, and many died from disease and poor conditions. Their descendants still make up much of the workforce on tea estates today, and campaigners continue to call for better wages and living conditions.

passages.title: Farming Goes Vertical
paragraphs: In a former warehouse on the edge of a city, rows of lettuce, basil and spinach grow in trays stacked from floor to ceiling. There is no soil and no sunlight, and the farmers wear lab coats rather than boots. This is a vertical farm, and over the past fifteen years such farms have been promoted as a way to grow fresh food close to the people who eat it, even in the most crowded cities.

Most vertical farms use a technique called hydroponics, in which plant roots sit in water containing all the nutrients the plants need. Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from LEDs, which can be tuned to produce exactly the colours of light that plants use most efficiently, while giving off relatively little heat. Temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels are controlled by computers, so that conditions remain ideal every day of the year.

Supporters point to impressive advantages. Because water is recycled within the system, vertical farms can use up to 95 percent less water than conventional fields. The sealed environment keeps out insects, so pesticides are unnecessary, and crops can be harvested all year round regardless of the weather. Because the farms are located in cities, produce can reach shops within hours of being picked, reducing waste and transport emissions.

The main problem is energy. Sunlight is free, but artificial light is not, and a vertical farm can consume enormous amounts of electricity. One estimate suggests that growing a kilogram of lettuce indoors may require many times more energy than growing it in a greenhouse. When electricity prices rose sharply in 2022, the costs of many farms soared.

The consequences were soon felt across the industry. In 2023, several high-profile vertical farming companies went bankrupt, despite having raised hundreds of millions of dollars from investors. Analysts concluded that many had expanded too quickly, building huge facilities before they had shown that their business could make a profit.

Few experts believe that vertical farms will replace conventional agriculture. Staple crops such as wheat and rice need too much space and light to be grown economically indoors. However, for fast-growing, perishable crops such as leafy greens and herbs, vertical farming may have a lasting role, especially where it can be powered by renewable energy. It is likely to be most valuable in places with little farmland or harsh climates, such as Singapore and parts of the Middle East.

passages.title: The Power of Habit
paragraphs: Much of what we do each day is not the result of careful decisions. We brush our teeth, check our phones and take the same route to work without really thinking about it. In a series of studies, the psychologist Wendy Wood asked participants to record what they were doing and thinking at regular intervals during the day. Around forty percent of their actions, she found, were performed almost automatically, while their minds were on something else.

Neuroscientists have identified a region deep in the brain, the basal ganglia, as central to this kind of automatic behaviour. When we first learn a task, such as driving a car, the brain works hard and we must concentrate on every step. With repetition, control gradually shifts to the basal ganglia, freeing the rest of the brain for other things. This is extremely efficient, but it also explains why bad habits are so hard to break: once a behaviour has become automatic, it no longer depends on our conscious intentions.

Popular books on the subject often describe habits in terms of a simple loop: a cue, such as a time of day or a feeling, triggers a routine, which is followed by a reward. Over time, the brain begins to expect the reward as soon as it notices the cue. The model is useful, but I think such books often make the process seem simpler than it is. Real habits are shaped by many overlapping cues, and the rewards involved are not always obvious.

One persistent myth is that it takes twenty-one days to form a new habit. There is no scientific basis for this figure. In a 2009 study at University College London, Phillippa Lally and her colleagues asked volunteers to adopt a new daily behaviour, such as eating a piece of fruit with lunch or going for a run before dinner. On average, it took 66 days before the behaviour felt automatic, but the range was enormous, from 18 to 254 days. Encouragingly, missing a single day did not significantly affect the process.

If habits are so powerful, how can we change them? Many people rely on willpower, but research suggests this is a poor strategy. Wood's work has found that people who appear to have strong self-control are not necessarily better at resisting temptation; instead, they tend to have built good habits that make resistance unnecessary. A more effective approach is to change the environment, making desirable behaviours easier and undesirable ones harder. Keeping fruit on the kitchen table and biscuits in a high cupboard is likely to achieve more than any amount of determination.

Major life changes can also provide an opportunity. When people move house or start a new job, the familiar cues that triggered their old habits disappear, and for a short period new behaviours are easier to establish. In my view, anyone hoping to change their habits should take advantage of such moments, rather than relying on motivation alone.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the main source of news for adults in one country between 2000 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Main source of news (% of adults)

model: The line graph shows the proportion of adults in one country who used television, newspapers, online sources and radio as their main source of news between 2000 and 2025.
Overall, online sources grew dramatically and replaced television as the most popular source, while all three traditional media declined, newspapers most sharply in relative terms.
In 2000, television was by far the dominant source of news, used by 62% of adults. Newspapers came second at 25%, followed by radio at 10%, while only 3% of people relied mainly on online sources.

Over the following 25 years, the figure for online news rose steadily, overtaking newspapers by 2010 and television by 2020, when it reached 52%. By 2025, it stood at 60%. Television, meanwhile, fell continuously to 30%, less than half its original level. The decline in newspapers was even steeper in relative terms, from 25% to just 5%. Radio remained stable at around 10% until 2010 but then dropped gradually to 5%.

task2.text: More and more people are now working from home rather than in an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Write at least 250 words.
model: Since the pandemic, working from home has changed from an unusual arrangement into a normal part of many people's lives. While this trend has some real drawbacks, I believe that, for most office workers, the advantages are greater.

The most obvious benefit is the time and money saved on commuting. In large cities, workers may spend two hours a day travelling, often in crowded and stressful conditions. Working from home gives this time back for rest, exercise or family. Many employees also report that they concentrate better without the interruptions of a busy office, and companies can save on the cost of renting large office spaces. In addition, fewer commuters means less traffic and pollution.

On the other hand, remote working can be isolating. Without casual conversations in the corridor, employees may feel disconnected from their colleagues, and young workers in particular may miss out on learning by watching more experienced staff. The boundary between work and home can also become blurred, leading some people to work longer hours and find it harder to switch off.

However, these problems can largely be solved by a hybrid approach, in which employees spend part of the week in the office. This allows teams to meet regularly for collaboration and training, while keeping most of the benefits of flexibility. Clear rules about working hours can also help protect people's free time.

In conclusion, although working from home has disadvantages, particularly for social contact and work-life balance, I believe its benefits for productivity, wellbeing and the environment outweigh them, especially when combined with some time in the office.

speaking.cue:
Describe a teacher who had a strong influence on you.
You should say:
- who this teacher was
- what subject they taught
- what they were like
and explain how they influenced you.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about my mathematics teacher in secondary school, Mr Rahman, who taught me for three years. Before I was in his class, I honestly thought I was bad at maths. I used to panic whenever I saw a difficult problem. What made him different was his patience. Instead of just giving us formulas to memorise, he always explained why a method worked, often using examples from everyday life, like calculating discounts in a shop or the speed of a cricket ball. He also had a habit of saying that mistakes were the most useful part of learning, and he'd sometimes ask us to explain our wrong answers to the class, which sounds frightening, but he did it in such a supportive way that nobody felt embarrassed. Gradually, my confidence grew, and by my final year maths had become my favourite subject. I think his influence goes beyond maths, actually. It's partly because of him that I chose to study computer science, and I still try to follow his approach: if I don't understand something, I keep asking why until it makes sense.
